title: Job-search strategy & role targeting
summary: Plan a focused job search: pick the right AI roles, read job descriptions critically, and build a pipeline you can track.
objectives: Distinguish ML engineer, data scientist, AI engineer and applied AI roles
Map your maths and L1 support background onto realistic entry points
Decode a job description to separate must-haves from nice-to-haves
Target roles by seniority, sector and tech stack instead of applying blindly
Build a simple application tracker and a weekly outreach routine
Tailor your CV keywords to each job using a repeatable process

quiz.q: You have a maths degree, L1 support experience and six months of Python and ML projects. Which role is usually the most realistic first target?
options: Junior or entry-level AI / data role
quiz.why: Entry-level and junior roles match a career-changer with projects but no commercial ML experience; senior and principal roles expect years of production work.

quiz.q: In a job description, what does the 'requirements' versus 'nice to have' split tell you?
quiz.answer: Requirements are the must-haves you should largely meet; nice-to-haves are bonus skills, so you can apply if you meet most requirements and a few extras.
quiz.why: Treating every bullet as mandatory makes you self-reject. Most candidates are hired without ticking every nice-to-have.

quiz.q: Roughly what overlap with the stated requirements is a sensible threshold for applying to an entry-level role?
options: Only apply at 90 percent or more
quiz.why: Around 60 to 70 percent overlap is a healthy signal; insisting on 100 percent means you apply far too little and miss roles you could grow into.

quiz.q: Why tailor CV keywords to each specific job description?
quiz.answer: Many employers use applicant tracking systems and keyword screens, so matching the language of the JD helps your CV pass filters and shows relevance.
quiz.why: An A T S and a busy recruiter both scan for the exact skills named in the posting; mirroring that language increases your hit rate.

quiz.q: Which is the better weekly habit for a 30-hour-a-week job seeker?
options: Send 50 generic applications in one burst
A steady routine of fewer, tailored applications plus outreach
Wait for recruiters to find you
Only apply when you feel fully qualified
quiz.why: A consistent pipeline of tailored applications and direct outreach converts far better than mass generic spraying or passive waiting.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of an application tracker?
quiz.answer: To record every role, its status and next action so you follow up on time, spot what is working and avoid duplicate or forgotten applications.
quiz.why: A tracker turns a chaotic search into a measurable pipeline you can review and improve each week.

body_markdown:
## Why strategy beats volume

A job search without a strategy means sending hundreds of generic applications and hearing nothing back. With only about thirty hours a week, you cannot out-spam the market — but you can out-target it. The goal of this lesson is a **focused pipeline**: the right roles, the right framing of your background, and a routine you can sustain.

You are a career-changer: a maths degree, an L1 support internship, and a growing portfolio of coding and machine-learning projects. That is a real, hireable profile — the job is to point it at the roles where it lands.

## Know the role landscape

AI job titles are messy and overlap. A few common buckets:

- **Data Scientist** — statistics, experiments, modelling, communicating insight.
- **Machine Learning Engineer** — building, training and shipping models in production.
- **AI / Applied AI Engineer** — wiring large language models and APIs into products.
- **Data / Analytics Engineer** — pipelines, SQL and the data plumbing underneath.

Your maths gives you an edge on the statistics-heavy roles; your support background gives you an edge anywhere that values communication and debugging under pressure. Target **junior** or **entry-level** versions first.

## Decode the job description

Most beginners self-reject by treating every bullet as mandatory. Read each posting in three passes: the **must-haves** (the requirements), the **nice-to-haves**, and the **signals** (sector, stack, team size). A useful rule of thumb: if you meet roughly sixty to seventy percent of the requirements, apply.

You can even score the overlap programmatically to keep yourself honest:

```python
jd_keywords = {"python", "sql", "pandas", "machine learning", "git", "aws"}
my_skills   = {"python", "sql", "pandas", "machine learning", "git"}

overlap = my_skills & jd_keywords
score = len(overlap) / len(jd_keywords)
print(f"Match: {score:.0%}  Missing: {jd_keywords - my_skills}")
# Match: 83%  Missing: {'aws'}
```

If you are at sixty percent or more, apply and name the one or two gaps as things you are actively learning.

## Build a trackable pipeline

Treat applications like a dataset. Capture every role, its status and the next action so nothing falls through the cracks. A spreadsheet works, but a tiny script keeps it consistent:

```bash
# one CSV per week; columns you actually review
echo "company,role,date_applied,status,next_action,follow_up_date" > applications.csv
echo "Acme,Junior Data Scientist,2026-06-15,applied,follow up,2026-06-22" >> applications.csv
cat applications.csv
```

Each week, review the tracker: which sources and which framings get replies? Double down on what works and drop what does not.

## A sustainable weekly routine

With thirty hours, protect a fixed rhythm: a block for **finding and tailoring** applications, a block for **outreach** (messaging people at target companies), and a block for **interview prep and projects**. Aim for a small number of well-tailored applications plus a few genuine messages each week, not a one-off burst of generic ones. Consistency compounds.

That is a genuinely hireable profile.

slides.narration: Here is where most beginners sabotage themselves. They read a job description, see one bullet they don't meet, and self-reject. Instead, read it in passes. First the must-haves, the actual requirements. Then the nice-to-haves, which are bonuses. Then the signals: the sector, the stack, the team size. Almost nobody hired ticks every single box.

slides.title: Score the overlap

About 60 to 70 percent overlap? Apply.
Name the one or two gaps as 'learning now'.
slides.narration: To stay honest, you can even score the overlap. Put the job's keywords in one set, your skills in another, and divide the intersection by the total. If you land around sixty to seventy percent or more, apply. In this example we match eighty percent, missing only A W S, which you'd simply name as something you're actively learning.

slides.narration: Let's recap. Win by targeting, not volume. Know the role landscape and aim at entry-level versions that fit your maths and support background. Decode each job description and apply when you meet most requirements, not all of them. And track everything so your search becomes a pipeline you can improve. Your task before the next lesson: build your application tracker and carefully tailor three applications. I'll see you next time, when we work on your C V.
